description: Solutions to data center water challenges, organized by actor type. Drawn from enacted legislation, utility programs, enforcement outcomes, and industry practice documented across the tracker's datasets.

categories.label: Policy & Regulatory Solutions
categories.description: Enacted laws, permits, and proposed rules that require or incentivize water-responsible data center siting, design, and reporting.

solutions.title: Virginia Monthly DC Water Reporting Mandate
solutions.actor: Virginia General Assembly / Dept. of Environmental Quality
solutions.description: HB 496 / SB 553 (enacted April 2026) requires water utilities to report monthly aggregate volumes delivered to data centers to the State Water Control Board. Creates the first mandatory utility-level data stream for DC water use in the US.
solutions.example: Loudoun Water (serving ~1.635B gal/yr to data centers) must file monthly reports beginning ~July 2026. First published data will be the only facility-aggregated DC water series in any US state.
solutions.cross_ref_note: VA HB 496 / SB 553 tracked in Legislation tab

solutions.title: Idaho Closed-Loop Cooling Mandate
solutions.description: H895 (enacted 2026) requires new data centers to use closed-loop or non-consumptive cooling systems as a permit condition, eliminating the largest evaporative water loss pathway. Designed to protect the Snake River Plain aquifer.
solutions.example: First state-level mandate of its kind in the US. South Carolina HB 4583 (pending) would extend this closed-loop model to the Southeast.
solutions.cross_ref_note: ID H895 and SC HB 4583 in Legislation tab

solutions.title: South Dakota Cost-Causation Billing
solutions.description: SB 135 (enacted 2026) requires data centers ≥10 MW to demonstrate water-supply compatibility and mandates that developers bear the marginal cost of supply-infrastructure expansions they trigger — not residential ratepayers.
solutions.example: Part of South Dakota's 'Data Center Bill of Rights.' Addresses the pattern where large industrial loads trigger regional water infrastructure upgrades whose costs are socialized to all ratepayers.

solutions.title: Utah Water Disclosure Law + Executive Order
solutions.description: HB 76 (enacted March 2026) mandates projected and actual water consumption disclosure from facilities ≥10,000 sq ft. EO 2026-03 (May 2026) directs agencies to require water-impact review before approvals and evaluate cost-attribution models.
solutions.example: Disclosure threshold set to match existing utility metering capabilities, making reporting immediately actionable rather than dependent on new infrastructure.
solutions.cross_ref_note: UT HB 76 and UT EO 2026-03 in Legislation tab

solutions.title: Ohio EPA Data Center Wastewater General Permit (OHD000001)
solutions.description: First proposed general permit requiring data centers to file Discharge Monitoring Reports (DMRs) directly for cooling-tower blowdown, closing the gap where DC cooling water routes through municipal WWTPs with no facility-level accounting.
solutions.example: Comment period closed January 2025; permit finalization pending as of June 2026. If enacted, it would create the first direct federal-level DC water monitoring dataset, complementing the WWTP-level data this project already tracks via EPA ECHO.
solutions.cross_ref_note: OHD000001 tracked by oh_epa_general_permit scraper — see Data tab

solutions.title: New York SEQRA Environmental Review for 50MW+ Facilities
solutions.description: S10642 / A11560 requires SEQRA environmental-impact assessment and public comment before any data center project exceeds 50 MW, including a mandatory water-supply analysis. Would be the broadest state environmental-review trigger for data centers in the US.
solutions.example: Passed Senate 44-16 and Assembly 102-39 as of June 2026. Gov. Hochul has not publicly committed to signing or vetoing.
solutions.cross_ref_note: NY S10642 / A11560 in Legislation tab

categories.label: Utility & Infrastructure Solutions
categories.description: Water utility programs and regional planning approaches that integrate data center demand into supply management, capacity planning, and dual-feed infrastructure.

solutions.title: Dual-Feed Systems: Potable + Reclaimed Water Connections
solutions.description: Data centers receive two separate connections — potable for human-contact uses and reclaimed (recycled, non-potable) water for cooling-tower makeup — reducing pressure on drinking water supplies.
solutions.example: Loudoun Water ACFR 2023: 899M gal potable + 736M gal reclaimed delivered to data centers annually. Reclaimed water is 45% of total DC supply — the highest reclaimed fraction of any US data center utility cluster tracked here.
solutions.cross_ref_note: Loudoun Water ACFR data tracked in Data tab

solutions.title: ERU-Based Demand Planning via Industrial User Surveys
solutions.description: Annual Industrial User Surveys allocate Equivalent Residential Units (ERUs) to data center customers, giving utility planners binding demand commitments for capital planning before construction begins.
solutions.example: 2024 survey: 56 data centers hold 3,276 ERUs = ~478M gal/yr (avg 58.5 ERU per facility). ERU allocations are reviewed with each expansion permit, creating a cumulative demand ledger that's used to size infrastructure upgrades.
solutions.cross_ref_note: Prince William Water IUS data in Data tab

solutions.title: Regional Demand Forecasting with Data Center Growth Scenarios
solutions.actor: Central Ohio Regional Water Authority / Ohio EPA
solutions.description: Collaborative regional water demand study incorporating data center growth scenarios to enable proactive infrastructure investment rather than reactive expansion after capacity constraints appear.
solutions.example: March 2025 study projects industrial demand: ~10 MGD (2024) → 40 MGD (2030) → 90 MGD (2050). Intel New Albany campus alone: ~6 MGD. Study is informing $2B+ in regional water infrastructure planning.
solutions.cross_ref_note: Central Ohio projections in Data tab

solutions.title: Aggregate DC Water Metering and Annual Public Reporting
solutions.description: Utilities publish aggregate data center water deliveries in annual financial reports (ACFRs), providing the only publicly available utility-level DC water volumes in Virginia — currently the primary Tier 1 data source for this tracker.
solutions.example: Loudoun Water ACFR 2023: 1.635B gal to data centers (~15% of total utility sales). Fairfax Water supplies ~18 MGD wholesale to Loudoun. Virginia HB 496 will formalize and extend this to monthly reports.
solutions.cross_ref_note: Loudoun Water and Fairfax Water data in Data tab

categories.label: Technology & Operational Solutions
categories.description: Engineering approaches that reduce or eliminate water consumption through improved cooling design, alternative water sources, and efficiency metrics.

solutions.title: Closed-Loop Recirculating Cooling Towers
solutions.actor: Hyperscalers (AWS, Google, Microsoft, Meta) — industry standard
solutions.description: Recirculating systems reuse the same water in a closed loop, dramatically reducing freshwater withdrawal compared to once-through systems. This is the current standard for all modern hyperscale facilities and the technology basis for Idaho's closed-loop mandate.
solutions.example: Typical WUE (Water Usage Effectiveness): 1.5–2.0 L/kWh for recirculating towers vs. 3–4 L/kWh for older designs. Industry target: WUE < 1.2 L/kWh. Still consumptive (evaporation) but far more efficient than alternatives.

solutions.title: Reclaimed / Recycled Water Sourcing
solutions.actor: Google (Prineville OR), Meta, Loudoun Water DC customers
solutions.description: Data centers contract with utilities or municipalities for reclaimed (non-potable recycled) water to supply cooling towers, freeing potable water for human use. Requires dual-plumbing infrastructure but is well-established in water-stressed regions.
solutions.example: Loudoun Water: 736M gal/yr reclaimed delivered to data centers (45% of total DC supply). Google's Prineville, OR campus uses 100% reclaimed water for cooling. Reclaimed water WUE is identical to potable — the gain is purely in source substitution.
solutions.cross_ref_note: Loudoun Water reclaimed volumes in Data tab

solutions.title: Direct Liquid Cooling (DLC) for AI / GPU Clusters
solutions.description: Liquid coolant is circulated directly to processors and server components, removing heat without relying on large evaporative cooling towers. Near-zero cooling water required for DLC-equipped racks — the cooling burden shifts to heat exchangers that can reject to ambient air.
solutions.example: Adoption accelerating for AI training clusters (H100/H200/GB200 GPU pods) where heat density exceeds air-side cooling limits. Microsoft reports WUE near 0 for full-DLC racks. At scale, eliminates the cooling-tower evaporation entirely.

solutions.title: Air-Side / Dry Cooling (Zero Evaporation)
solutions.actor: Microsoft (Dublin, Ireland; Helsinki, Finland), UK operators
solutions.description: In cooler climates, outside air rejects heat without any water evaporation — 'free cooling' or 'economizer mode.' Zero consumptive water use when operating in full air-side mode. Feasibility depends on wet-bulb temperature and local climate.
solutions.example: Microsoft's Dublin data center uses air-side cooling 95%+ of the year, achieving near-zero WUE. Not viable for Virginia summer conditions without backup wet cooling; becomes more viable for data centers sited in northern latitudes or at altitude.

solutions.title: Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) Self-Reporting
solutions.actor: Green Grid (standard-setter), Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon
solutions.description: WUE (liters of water per kilowatt-hour of IT load) is an industry self-reporting metric enabling year-over-year comparison. Analogous to PUE for power efficiency, it allows tracking progress without facility-level disclosure — though no independent verification exists.
solutions.example: Google 2024: WUE 1.10 L/kWh (global average). Microsoft FY2023: WUE 0.33 L/kWh (includes 'net-water replenishments' — accounting treatment disputed). Meta: 0.26 L/kWh. No independent auditor verifies these figures — see Company Claims tab for verbatim operator quotes.
solutions.cross_ref_note: Company Claims in Legislation tab (Company Water Claims section)

solutions.title: Immersion Cooling (Full Liquid Submersion)
solutions.actor: Submer, Wiwynn, GRC, early Microsoft pilots
solutions.description: Servers are fully submerged in dielectric (non-conductive) fluid that absorbs heat directly. The fluid is cooled via compact heat exchangers that can reject to ambient air with minimal or zero evaporative water loss — potentially eliminating cooling water entirely at scale.
solutions.example: Commercial deployments remain rare at hyperscale as of 2026, primarily in HPC and crypto mining. Microsoft and others have published pilot results. Long-term potential to reduce WUE to ~0 without requiring a cold climate or DLC-compatible processor packages.
